add.text:
Read this numbered, cleaned transcript of the owner talking. Turn it into an outline a reader
takes in at a glance: "tangible, familiar, easy to digest". The owner's words for it: "putting
familiar names, like the headings" on the thing being discussed and on each of its parts.

Output Markdown in EXACTLY this shape:

# <the concrete thing being discussed>
## <a familiar name for one part of it>
- <one point, in the owner's own words> [S#, S#]
  - <a detail or example of that point, only if it needs its own line> [S#]
## <the next part>
- <...> [S#]

Rules:
- The H1 is CONCRETE: a thing a reader could point at — a class, a page, a tab, a tool, a feature
  (the owner's example: "Page class"). Never an abstract category like "AI processes", "Thoughts"
  or "Feedback". If the transcript covers several separate things, name them plainly in the one
  H1 ("Page class and Sidebar") and give each its own H2 or H2s.
- Exactly ONE "#" H1. One "##" H2 per distinct part — never invent one just to have more.
- Each H2 is a FAMILIAR name a reader already knows. If a name already exists for that part (the
  owner's example: "Layout"), use that exact name; otherwise use the owner's own word for it.
- ONE BULLET PER POINT, NOT PER SENTENCE. When several sentences make one point (a claim, its
  reason, "so I like that"), merge them into one bullet, a short line in the owner's own words,
  citing every one of those sentences. Filler that makes no point of its own ("Couple of things.")
  gets no bullet: add its number to the nearest bullet's citation instead.
- AT MOST TWO LEVELS: a bullet, and sub-bullets under it. Never a third level.
- KEEP EVERY POINT. Merging sentences that make the same point is required; dropping a point is
  not allowed. Never turn a hedge ("maybe", "I think", "I guess") into a flat claim.
- Cite EVERY sentence number EXACTLY ONCE, in the one bullet where its main point went — never
  under two headings. Form: [S3, S7], each number individually, never a range like [S6-S9]. Use
  only numbers that appear below.

STYLE of anything the owner will read (the owner's rules):
- It is an OVERVIEW of what was said, in the owner's own key words. Never the whole rant, never a retelling.
- Each point has its answer or action baked in: say what is done, what to do, or what is still open. Do not invent an answer the transcript or the facts do not give; mark such a point open instead.
- Order by dependency and ease: clarifications and quick items first, then what depends on them. If neither applies, keep the owner's order.
- Reuse the same names for the same things every time, so they become familiar, and always name the context (the page, class, module or session) a point belongs to.
- Headings are big: "#" for the one subject, "##" for each part, "###" only when a part truly needs a split. Never "####" or smaller. Every heading starts with one fitting emoji icon.
- Under a heading: short titled lists. A status bullet starts with ✅ (done) or ⬜ (not done) when the status is known; otherwise a plain "-" bullet. Few emoji, never decoration.
- Every card cites the clean-sentence numbers it came from, like [S3, S7], each number individually.
Apply this to the headings and bullets of the outline.

Cleaned transcript:
"""
S1. Yeah, so I think that can be a dynamic situation.
S2. I don't think there's necessarily one rule set, and so we'll have to tweak that and maybe have, I don't know, some sort of flow chart or document to try and figure out how to do that.
S3. Okay, so yeah, not interrupting me.
S4. It's like when you get a message, kind of randomly asynchronously, the default is you just add that message to the chart
S5. Now, the problem is if I'm in the middle of talking, obviously we want to suppress maybe even the display of your messages.
S6. I think it's a little bit more polite to not throw a new message at me while I'm talking.
S7. So, yeah, that's definitely a thing there.
S8. And then in terms of waiting to respond, one to two seconds is probably too much because then when you're trying to have a quick conversation.
S9. But I think sometimes I'll inflect my voice at the end of a question and then stop and then it's a little bit more obvious.
S10. I think sometimes when I'm in the middle of a long transcription, I might take a pause to think and it might be less obvious.
S11. I'm not sure of a lot of things.
S12. Number one, how often is the smart assistant here?
S13. Well, you are, you're the smart assistant, right?
S14. How often are you getting my transcriptions?
S15. I think maybe we're still chunking them into these big chunks.
S16. It seems that it's waiting for two or three second delay before it sends it.
S17. And if that's the case, we might want to change that.
S18. One thing that I've thought about is, while I'm talking, you could be already looking into the first things that I've been saying.
S19. So if I were to send an update to this live transcription that I'm doing right now, every sentence instead of in a big bulk batch of 20 sentences after a long pause, you could be doing work in the background.
S20. Now, how you do that work in order to stay hands-free so that you're able to respond to me quickly, I think really almost gets us back to having a fast assistant and a smart assistant so that a smart assistant can be kind of working, maybe getting his hands a little dirty in the background, whereas the smart assistant is able to respond immediately to findings.
S21. And so I don't know, I'm not sure exactly how that should work.
S22. Now when we have this voice mode, it adds another little complication to it because the formatting and the creation and the timing of these messages needs to happen properly.
S23. But one thing that I was thinking is, okay, so number one, if you're interjecting, well, I mean, yeah, I guess having conditional modes, I'm just thinking it kind of depends at different times.
S24. I do think interjections could be a little bit more, start with, well, no, I think generally speaking, if you stop talking during a transcription
S25. So here's one thing that I'm thinking.
S26. The AI generally generates these responses token by token and streams them.
S27. I'm not sure exactly how many tokens per second these models are responding.
S28. These are Claude Code models essentially, or Claude models, and how quickly they're responding.
S29. One sort of thought here though is, as the message is being generated, it's being read aloud and it's probably generating it faster than it's reading aloud.
S30. However, what I was thinking is that we could kind of go back to slow generation mode, but more or less, instead of generating the entire passage all at once, it's and then reading it aloud slowly, we could make it at least look like the message is being read kind of in real time
S31. And so each new word would appear on the screen as, maybe a little bit before it's being said so that you can kind of have a little bit of premonition when it comes.
S32. However, then when I interject, or if in the case that you interrupt yourself, however the voice stops reading, we need to be able to track what was read aloud.
S33. Because, and not even having that mode where you don't even show the rest of it
S34. And also then if the UI can send an interrupt, message to your session, then you get the feedback, okay, this was the last word that was read aloud, for example.
S35. So I don't know the best way to encode that, but the idea is that the, well, okay, this it's a little complicated, you could note this down as a potential solution is that you if you had a second agent, where one agent only gets the, and the last word spoken, and doesn't even get the rest of the message, then that agent could be essentially given the user's prompts
S36. And then at the end of the system, the LLM's response, either if it made it to the end or at the interrupt point, and it's essentially only putting into context the things that were actually read aloud.
S37. And the reason for that is that then you'd never have this problem where, hey, I already told you that, but you'd never heard it.
S38. And I never knew that you didn't hear it.
S39. And so then something that was said is just assumed to have been heard, but it was never heard.
S40. And so it just gets lost in context.
S41. So doing this, it would be a special mode.
S42. It might actually eat more tokens, but the one advantage of it is that the next prompt essentially, well, it's basically the unfinished AI message is stripped from the context for the next prompt.
S43. So maybe it doesn't really even require forking another parallel agent or whatever, maybe we just set up a script via the SDK where we can strip the unspoken part of the response from the next turn so that then the LLM knows, oh, well, you didn't get what, well, it was, I don't know if it, yeah, it'd probably be followed with an interrupt
S44. So it knows that it never finished its thought.
S45. And so then it can re-identify those things later automatically.
S46. I think that could be a cool feature.
S47. I'm not sure exactly how you pass that along.
"""

Output ONLY the Markdown described above (the H1, its H2s, and their bullets), nothing else.
